gas: the invisible water vapour above a boiling kettle
the air in a soccer ball
the air inside a bubble-gum bubble
the helium in a party balloon
the air inside a bike tire
the air in a beach ball

STATE_FACTS.q: Which is the coldest?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Numbers below zero are colder than zero.
STATE_FACTS.why: −10 °C is below freezing, so it is the coldest.

STATE_FACTS.q: What tool do we use to measure temperature?
STATE_FACTS.hint: It has a red or silver line that goes up when it is warm.
STATE_FACTS.why: A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius.

STATE_FACTS.q: Which is the hottest?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Look for the biggest number.
STATE_FACTS.why: 100 °C is the hottest of these.

STATE_FACTS.q: What is the gas that we breathe all around us called?
STATE_FACTS.hint: You fill balloons with it.
STATE_FACTS.why: Air is a mix of gases all around us.

STATE_FACTS.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Think of an ice cube versus water.
STATE_FACTS.why: A solid has a definite shape and volume.

STATE_FACTS.q: Which state of matter takes the shape of its container but keeps the same amount (volume)?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Pour juice from a tall glass into a bowl.
STATE_FACTS.why: A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.

STATE_FACTS.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Think about the air in a room.
STATE_FACTS.why: A gas has no definite shape or volume. It expands to fill its container.

STATE_FACTS.q: When ice turns into water, it is called…
STATE_FACTS.hint: Ice cream does this on a hot day.
STATE_FACTS.why: Solid to liquid is melting.

STATE_FACTS.q: When water turns into ice, it is called…
STATE_FACTS.hint: It happens to ponds in an Alberta winter.
STATE_FACTS.why: Liquid to solid is freezing.

STATE_FACTS.q: When a puddle dries up in the sun, the water is…
STATE_FACTS.hint: The water turns into a gas and goes into the air.
STATE_FACTS.why: Liquid to gas is evaporation.

STATE_FACTS.q: Water drops form on the outside of a cold glass. This is…
STATE_FACTS.hint: Water vapour in the air touches something cold.
STATE_FACTS.why: Gas to liquid is condensation.

STATE_FACTS.q: At what temperature does water freeze?
STATE_FACTS.hint: It is the same temperature at which ice melts.
STATE_FACTS.why: Water freezes and melts at 0 °C.

STATE_FACTS.q: At what temperature does water boil?
STATE_FACTS.hint: It is much hotter than a hot bath.
STATE_FACTS.why: Water boils at 100 °C.

STATE_FACTS.q: Does water melt and freeze at the same temperature?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Ice melts at 0 °C. Water freezes at…?
STATE_FACTS.why: Melting and freezing happen at the same temperature.

STATE_FACTS.q: What do we need to add to make ice melt?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Put an ice cube in your warm hand.
STATE_FACTS.why: Heating makes solids melt; cooling makes liquids freeze.

STATE_FACTS.q: Does matter take up space and have weight?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Even air takes up space: think of a balloon.
STATE_FACTS.why: All matter takes up space and has weight.

STATE_FACTS.q: What happens to most solids when you heat them enough?
w: they turn into gas right away
STATE_FACTS.hint: Think of butter in a hot pan.
STATE_FACTS.why: Enough heat makes most solids melt.

STATE_FACTS.q: The outdoor rink is −5 °C. Will the ice stay frozen?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Water freezes at 0 °C.
STATE_FACTS.why: Below 0 °C, water stays frozen.

STATE_FACTS.q: It is 12 °C on a spring day. What happens to a snowman?
w: it turns into steam right away
STATE_FACTS.hint: 12 °C is warmer than 0 °C.
STATE_FACTS.why: Above 0 °C, snow and ice melt.

STATE_FACTS.q: What happens when you cool water vapour?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Think of drops on a cold window.
STATE_FACTS.why: Cooling a gas turns it back into a liquid. That is condensation.

STATE_FACTS.q: Why does a pot of soup steam when it is hot?
STATE_FACTS.a: some of the water is evaporating
STATE_FACTS.hint: Hot liquid water turns into a gas.
STATE_FACTS.why: Heat makes water evaporate into steam.

STATE_FACTS.q: Can water be a solid, a liquid and a gas?
STATE_FACTS.a: yes: ice, water and water vapour
w: no, water is only a liquid
only a liquid and a solid
STATE_FACTS.hint: Think of an ice cube, a glass of water and steam.
STATE_FACTS.why: Water can be ice (solid), water (liquid) or vapour (gas).

STATE_FACTS.q: Why do people put salt on icy sidewalks?
w: salt makes the sidewalk warmer than the sun
STATE_FACTS.hint: Salty ice melts below 0 °C.
STATE_FACTS.why: Salt helps ice melt, but it works best when it is not very cold. Calgary also spreads sand and gravel for grip.

STATE_FACTS.q: Which state of matter can be squeezed into a much smaller space?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Think of air in a bike pump.
STATE_FACTS.why: The bits of a gas are far apart, so a gas can be squeezed. Solids and liquids hardly squeeze at all.

STATE_FACTS.q: Ice cubes float in a glass of water. Is the ice still water?
STATE_FACTS.a: yes, it is water as a solid
STATE_FACTS.hint: What happens when it melts?
STATE_FACTS.why: Ice is just frozen water.

STATE_FACTS.q: A chinook blows into Calgary and it goes from −15 °C to 8 °C. What happens to the snow?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Is 8 °C above or below freezing?
STATE_FACTS.why: Warm chinook winds raise the temperature above 0 °C, so snow melts.

STATE_FACTS.q: When chocolate melts and then cools again, what happens?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Melting can be undone by cooling.
STATE_FACTS.why: Cooling a melted solid makes it freeze back into a solid.

STATE_FACTS.q: Your body temperature is about…
STATE_FACTS.hint: It is warm, but not as hot as boiling water.
STATE_FACTS.why: A healthy body is about 37 °C.

STATE_FACTS.q: Which change needs heat to be taken away?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Think of a freezer.
STATE_FACTS.why: Freezing happens when a liquid is cooled.

STATE_FACTS.q: Which change needs heat to be added?
STATE_FACTS.hint: Think of the sun drying a puddle.
STATE_FACTS.why: Heat makes liquids evaporate.

STATE_FACTS.q: Why does a balloon get bigger when you blow into it?
STATE_FACTS.a: the gas spreads out to fill it
STATE_FACTS.hint: Gases fill whatever space they are in.
STATE_FACTS.why: The air you blow in spreads out and pushes the balloon wider.

WATER.q: What makes water evaporate from lakes and oceans?
WATER.hint: What warms the Earth?
WATER.why: The sun heats water and it evaporates into water vapour.

WATER.q: Clouds are made of…
WATER.a: tiny drops of water or ice
WATER.hint: Water vapour cools and condenses high in the sky.
WATER.why: Clouds form when water vapour condenses into tiny drops.

WATER.q: Rain, snow and hail are all kinds of…
WATER.hint: It is water falling from clouds.
WATER.why: Water falling from clouds is precipitation.

WATER.q: Where does water go after it falls as rain?
WATER.a: into rivers, lakes, oceans and the ground
WATER.hint: Think about puddles and rivers after a storm.
WATER.why: Water collects on land and in bodies of water, then the cycle repeats.

WATER.q: In an Alberta winter, many lakes…
WATER.hint: People skate on them.
WATER.why: In winter many water surfaces freeze, and in spring they thaw.

WATER.q: Is it safe to walk on a lake in early spring when the ice is melting?
WATER.hint: Ice gets thinner as it melts.
WATER.why: Melting ice is thin and dangerous. Stay off it.

WATER.q: What is water vapour?
w: a kind of cloud you can touch
WATER.hint: It is in the air all around us, but we cannot see it.
WATER.why: Water vapour is water in its gas state.

WATER.q: Snow in the Rocky Mountains melts in spring. Where does that water go?
WATER.a: into streams and rivers like the Bow
WATER.hint: Water flows downhill.
WATER.why: Meltwater runs into streams and rivers, and the cycle keeps going.

WATER.q: Why does a puddle dry up faster on a hot day than a cool day?
w: puddles are scared of the sun
WATER.hint: What does the sun add?
WATER.why: More heat means faster evaporation.

WATER.q: Is the water you drink today the same water that has been on Earth for a very long time?
w: no, new water is made every day
no, water is made in factories
WATER.hint: That is why it is called a cycle.
WATER.why: Earth’s water moves round and round in the water cycle.

WATER.q: Hail is…
WATER.a: balls of ice that fall from storm clouds
WATER.hint: Calgary gets lots of it in summer storms.
WATER.why: Hail is precipitation made of ice.

WATER.q: Fog is like…
WATER.hint: You can walk through it.
WATER.why: Fog is tiny water drops floating near the ground, just like a low cloud.

WATER.q: Why does snow fall in winter instead of rain?
WATER.a: it is cold enough for the water to freeze
WATER.hint: What temperature does water freeze at?
WATER.why: Below 0 °C, precipitation falls as snow.

WATER.q: Which part of the water cycle makes clouds?
WATER.hint: Vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops.
WATER.why: Condensation turns water vapour into the drops that make clouds.

WATER.q: Which part of the water cycle is rain falling?
WATER.hint: Water falls from the clouds.
WATER.why: Rain, snow and hail are precipitation.

WATER.q: Which part of the water cycle is a lake drying up in the sun?
WATER.hint: Liquid water turns into a gas.
WATER.why: Evaporation turns liquid water into water vapour.

WATER.q: Which part of the water cycle is rain running into a river?
WATER.hint: Water gathers together again.
WATER.why: Water collecting in rivers, lakes and oceans is collection.

WATER.q: Why should we keep rivers and lakes clean?
WATER.a: all living things need clean water
WATER.hint: Who drinks the water?
WATER.why: People, plants and animals all depend on clean water.

WATER.q: What do we call water that soaks into the ground?
WATER.hint: It is under the ground.
WATER.why: Water that soaks into soil and rock is groundwater.

WATER.q: What makes water in a cloud fall as rain?
WATER.a: the drops join up and get too heavy
WATER.hint: Tiny drops bump together and grow.
WATER.why: When cloud drops grow too heavy, they fall as precipitation.

WATER.q: Where is most of Earth’s water?
WATER.hint: Look at a globe. What colour covers most of it?
WATER.why: Most of Earth’s water is salty ocean water.

WATER.q: Why can’t we drink ocean water?
WATER.hint: Taste the sea and you will know.
WATER.why: Ocean water has too much salt for people to drink.

WATER.q: Where does Calgary get its drinking water?
WATER.a: from the Bow and Elbow rivers
WATER.hint: Two rivers flow through the city.
WATER.why: Calgary cleans water from the Bow and Elbow rivers.

WATER.q: What happens to snow on the ground in spring?
WATER.a: it melts and flows into streams or soaks into the ground
w: it flies back into the clouds right away
WATER.hint: Spring is warmer.
WATER.why: Melting snow joins rivers and groundwater.

WATER.q: Why are there drops on the grass early in the morning?
WATER.a: water vapour condensed on the cool grass
w: it rained in the night for sure
a sprinkler did it every time
WATER.hint: The grass is cool after the night.
WATER.why: That water is dew. Vapour in the air condenses on cool surfaces.

WATER.q: What does the water cycle need to keep going?
WATER.hint: What heats the water?
WATER.why: The sun’s heat drives evaporation, which keeps the cycle moving.

WATER.q: A cloud gets dark and grey before a storm because…
WATER.a: it is full of lots of water drops
WATER.hint: Thick clouds block more sunlight.
WATER.why: Big storm clouds hold lots of water, so less light gets through.

WATER.q: Which way does water flow in a river?
WATER.hint: Think about water poured on a slide.
WATER.why: Gravity pulls water downhill.

WATER.q: Which of these is a way to save water?
WATER.a: turning off the tap while brushing your teeth
w: watering the lawn in the rain
WATER.hint: Do not let water run when you are not using it.
WATER.why: Saving water keeps more clean water for everyone.

WATER.q: Snow is a kind of…
WATER.hint: It falls from clouds.
WATER.why: Snow is frozen precipitation.

WATER.q: What turns into water vapour when it is heated by the sun?
WATER.a: water in lakes, rivers and oceans
WATER.hint: It is a liquid.
WATER.why: Liquid water evaporates when it is heated.

WATER.q: A glacier is part of the water cycle because…
WATER.a: it stores water as ice and melts slowly
WATER.hint: Glaciers are frozen water.
WATER.why: Glaciers hold water as ice and release it as meltwater.

WATER.q: Plants are part of the water cycle because they…
WATER.a: give off water vapour from their leaves
WATER.hint: Leaves breathe out a little water.
WATER.why: Plants release water vapour into the air.

WATER.q: Rain soaks into the soil. Who uses that water next?
WATER.hint: What drinks from the ground?
WATER.why: Roots take up water from the soil.

NATURAL.q: Paper is made from which natural material?
NATURAL.hint: Paper mills use logs.
NATURAL.why: Paper is processed from wood.

NATURAL.q: Glass is made from which natural material?
NATURAL.hint: You find lots of it at the beach.
NATURAL.why: Glass is made by melting sand.

NATURAL.q: A wool sweater comes from…
NATURAL.hint: Which animal grows a fleece?
NATURAL.why: Wool is a natural material from sheep. People spin it into yarn.

NATURAL.q: Cheese is processed from…
NATURAL.hint: It comes from cows, goats or sheep.
NATURAL.why: Cheese is made from milk.

NATURAL.q: Bricks are made from…
NATURAL.hint: It is a kind of soft earth that gets baked hard.
NATURAL.why: Bricks are baked clay.

NATURAL.q: Bread is made from…
NATURAL.hint: Alberta farmers grow a lot of it.
NATURAL.why: Flour for bread comes from wheat.

NATURAL.q: Which of these is a natural material?
NATURAL.hint: Natural materials are found in nature, not made in a factory.
NATURAL.why: A rock is natural. The others are processed.

NATURAL.q: Which of these is a processed material?
NATURAL.hint: Processed materials are changed by people and are not found in nature.
NATURAL.why: Plastic is made in factories, so it is processed.

NATURAL.q: A leather baseball glove is made from…
NATURAL.hint: Leather comes from cows.
NATURAL.why: Leather is processed from animal hides.

NATURAL.q: A cotton T-shirt comes from…
NATURAL.hint: Cotton grows in fluffy balls on a bush.
NATURAL.why: Cotton is a natural fibre from the cotton plant.

NATURAL.q: Which of these natural materials comes from an animal?
NATURAL.hint: It grows on an animal.
NATURAL.why: Wool is natural. It comes from sheep.

NATURAL.q: A metal spoon is made from metal that was dug out of…
NATURAL.hint: Miners dig for it.
NATURAL.why: Metals come from ores, which are rocks.

NATURAL.q: Why do we make some materials, like plastic?
NATURAL.a: to get properties we need, like waterproof and light
NATURAL.hint: Think of a raincoat or a water bottle.
NATURAL.why: People process materials to give them useful properties.

NATURAL.q: Which material would be best for a window?
NATURAL.a: glass, because you can see through it
NATURAL.hint: A window needs to let light in.
NATURAL.why: Glass is transparent, so it is good for windows.

NATURAL.q: Which material would be best for a winter mitten?
NATURAL.hint: Mittens need to keep your hands warm.
NATURAL.why: Wool keeps heat in.

NATURAL.q: Which is a way to reuse a material?
NATURAL.a: using a glass jar to hold crayons
w: throwing the jar in the garbage
NATURAL.hint: Give it a new job.
NATURAL.why: Reusing gives materials a second life.

NATURAL.q: Recycling paper means…
NATURAL.hint: It goes in the blue bin.
NATURAL.why: Recycled paper is processed into new paper products.

NATURAL.q: Maple syrup is processed from…
NATURAL.hint: People tap trees in early spring.
NATURAL.why: Sap is boiled down to make maple syrup.

NATURAL.q: Rubber for boots first comes from…
NATURAL.hint: It drips out of a tree like syrup.
NATURAL.why: Natural rubber is made from tree sap.

NATURAL.q: A wooden hockey stick was made from…
NATURAL.hint: Wood comes from…
NATURAL.why: Wood is a natural material from trees. People cut and shape it.

NATURAL.q: Silk is a natural material made by…
NATURAL.hint: It is spun by a little caterpillar.
NATURAL.why: Silkworms spin silk threads.

NATURAL.q: Which would be the best material for a raincoat?
NATURAL.a: a waterproof material like plastic or rubber
NATURAL.hint: Rain needs to roll off.
NATURAL.why: Waterproof materials keep you dry.

NATURAL.q: Which would be the best material for a goalie’s water bottle?
NATURAL.a: plastic, because it is light and will not break
NATURAL.hint: It might get dropped on the ice.
NATURAL.why: Plastic is light and unbreakable, so it is good for sports bottles.

NATURAL.q: Concrete for sidewalks is made by mixing…
NATURAL.hint: It starts wet and gets hard as stone.
NATURAL.why: Concrete is a processed material made from rock materials.

NATURAL.q: Butter is processed from…
NATURAL.hint: It is shaken or churned.
NATURAL.why: Butter is made by churning cream.

NATURAL.q: Jam is processed from…
NATURAL.hint: Think of strawberries.
NATURAL.why: Jam is cooked fruit and sugar.

NATURAL.q: Which material would make the best snow shovel?
NATURAL.hint: It must be strong and not break.
NATURAL.why: Strong, light materials are good for shovels.

NATURAL.q: Why are frying pans made of metal?
NATURAL.a: metal passes heat to the food and can take high heat
w: metal is light as a feather
NATURAL.hint: The pan has to get hot.
NATURAL.why: Metal carries heat well and does not melt on a stove.

NATURAL.q: Traditional Indigenous birchbark canoes were made from…
NATURAL.hint: The name tells you.
NATURAL.why: Birchbark is a strong, light, natural material.

NATURAL.q: Which material is see-through?
NATURAL.hint: Windows are made of it.
NATURAL.why: Glass lets light through, so we can see through it.

NATURAL.q: Which material is the best to make a warm blanket?
NATURAL.hint: It comes from sheep.
NATURAL.why: Wool traps heat and keeps you warm.

reversible: squishing play dough into a ball
dissolving sugar in water and letting it dry
melting a crayon and letting it cool
freezing apple juice and letting it melt
melting ice cubes and freezing them again
dissolving salt in water and letting the water dry up
melting snow in a pot and freezing it again
permanent: a log burning in a campfire

FORCES.q: A force is a…
FORCES.hint: Think about what you do to open a door.
FORCES.why: A force is a push or a pull.

FORCES.q: You kick a soccer ball. What kind of force is that?
FORCES.hint: Your foot moves the ball away from you.
FORCES.why: Kicking pushes the ball away.

FORCES.q: You open a drawer toward you. What kind of force is that?
FORCES.hint: The drawer comes toward you.
FORCES.why: Pulling brings something toward you.

FORCES.q: Why is it hard to slide a box across a carpet?
FORCES.hint: It is the force between two surfaces rubbing.
FORCES.why: Friction slows things that rub together.

FORCES.q: Why does a puck slide farther on ice than on grass?
FORCES.hint: Smooth, slippery surfaces have less of something.
FORCES.why: Ice is smooth, so there is less friction to slow the puck.

FORCES.q: A puck is sitting still on the ice. What will make it move?
FORCES.a: a force, like a hit from a stick
FORCES.hint: Objects stay still until a force acts on them.
FORCES.why: Objects stay still or keep moving until a force acts on them.

FORCES.q: Pulling on a rope in tug of war makes what kind of force in the rope?
FORCES.hint: The rope is pulled tight from both ends.
FORCES.why: A pulled rope or string has tension.

FORCES.q: A stretched slingshot band pushing back is what kind of force?
FORCES.hint: Things like springs and rubber bands bounce back.
FORCES.why: Springs and rubber bands make elastic forces.

FORCES.q: What can a force do to a moving object?
FORCES.hint: Think of a goalie, a stick and a boot.
FORCES.why: Forces can speed things up, slow or stop them, or change their direction.

FORCES.q: Squeezing play dough shows that a force can change an object’s…
FORCES.hint: What happens to the dough?
FORCES.why: Forces can change the shape or size of objects.

FORCES.q: What force pulls a ball back down after you throw it up?
FORCES.hint: It pulls everything toward the ground.
FORCES.why: Gravity pulls objects toward Earth.

FORCES.q: Sand on an icy sidewalk helps you not slip because it adds…
FORCES.hint: Rough surfaces grip better.
FORCES.why: Sand makes the surface rougher, so there is more friction.

FORCES.q: A goalie stops a moving puck. The force changed the puck’s…
FORCES.hint: It was moving, now it is not.
FORCES.why: Forces can stop moving objects.

FORCES.q: A magnet pulls a paper clip without touching it. This force is…
FORCES.hint: Fridge magnets use it.
FORCES.why: Magnets can push or pull some metals without touching them.

FORCES.q: A trampoline bouncing you up is an example of…
FORCES.hint: It stretches and springs back.
FORCES.why: Stretchy things push back with elastic force.

FORCES.q: Why do skis have smooth, waxed bottoms?
FORCES.a: to lower friction so they glide
FORCES.hint: Smooth surfaces slide easily.
FORCES.why: Wax makes the skis smoother, which lowers friction.

FORCES.q: Pulling a kite string tight on a windy day makes…
FORCES.hint: The string is pulled from both ends.
FORCES.why: A tight string or rope has tension.

FORCES.q: Which would need the biggest push to move?
FORCES.hint: Heavier things need more force.
FORCES.why: Heavier objects need a bigger force to move.

FORCES.q: You push a toy car softly, then hard. When does it go farther?
w: it goes the same both times
FORCES.hint: A bigger force makes a bigger change.
FORCES.why: A bigger push gives the car more motion.

FORCES.q: What makes a moving hockey puck slow down and stop by itself?
FORCES.hint: Even ice has a tiny bit of rubbing.
FORCES.why: Friction slowly slows the puck.

FORCES.q: A soccer ball is rolling. A player kicks it from the side. What changes?
FORCES.hint: Where is it going now?
FORCES.why: A force can change the direction of a moving object.

FORCES.q: Which surface has the MOST friction for a sled?
FORCES.hint: Rough surfaces rub more.
FORCES.why: Rough surfaces like gravel have lots of friction.

FORCES.q: Why do winter tires have deep, bumpy treads?
FORCES.a: to add friction on snow and ice
w: to make the car go uphill only
FORCES.hint: They need to grip the road.
FORCES.why: Deep treads grip slippery roads by adding friction.

FORCES.q: Do magnets attract wood?
FORCES.a: no, only some metals like iron
FORCES.hint: Try a fridge magnet on a pencil.
FORCES.why: Magnets attract some metals, like iron and steel, but not wood.

FORCES.q: The two ends of a magnet are called…
FORCES.hint: North and south…
FORCES.why: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

FORCES.q: Two magnets push apart. What must be facing each other?
FORCES.a: the same poles, like north and north
FORCES.hint: Same poles push away. Different poles pull together.
FORCES.why: Like poles repel each other.

FORCES.q: A ball sits still on the floor. What forces are acting on it?
FORCES.a: gravity pulls down and the floor pushes up
FORCES.hint: Gravity never turns off.
FORCES.why: Balanced forces keep the ball still.

FORCES.q: Which can a force change?
FORCES.hint: Think of kicking, steering and squishing.
FORCES.why: Forces can change how fast, which way, and the shape of things.

FORCES.q: Why is it easier to slide in socks on a wood floor than on a carpet?
FORCES.hint: Smooth surfaces rub less.
FORCES.why: Smooth wood has less friction than rough carpet.

FORCES.q: A hockey player taps a puck gently. Then she takes a slapshot. Which force is bigger?
FORCES.hint: Which one makes the puck go faster?
FORCES.why: A bigger force makes the puck move faster.

FORCES.q: What happens if you stop pedalling your bike on flat ground?
FORCES.hint: Something is rubbing on the wheels and road.
FORCES.why: Friction slows the bike down.

FORCES.q: A diver jumps off a diving board and falls into the pool. Which force pulls the diver down?
FORCES.hint: It pulls everything toward Earth.
FORCES.why: Gravity pulls the diver down.

FORCES.q: A stretched rubber band is let go. What does it do?
FORCES.a: it snaps back to its shape
FORCES.hint: Rubber is stretchy.
FORCES.why: Elastic materials spring back after stretching.

MACHINES.q: A ramp used to roll a heavy box into a truck is a…
MACHINES.hint: It is a sloped surface.
MACHINES.why: A ramp is an inclined plane. It lets you use less force over a longer distance.

MACHINES.q: A seesaw is a…
MACHINES.hint: It is a bar that turns on a point.
MACHINES.why: A seesaw is a lever. It turns on a point called a fulcrum.

MACHINES.q: A wagon uses which simple machine to roll easily?
MACHINES.hint: Look under the wagon.
MACHINES.why: Wheels on an axle make moving loads easier.

MACHINES.q: Why do people use simple machines?
MACHINES.hint: Think about carrying a heavy load with or without a wagon.
MACHINES.why: Simple machines reduce the effort needed to move things.

MACHINES.q: A paddle pushing a canoe through water works like a…
MACHINES.hint: You hold it and it turns as you pull.
MACHINES.why: A paddle is a lever. First Nations peoples designed paddles and still use them.

MACHINES.q: An ulu is a curved knife used by Inuit. Its blade is a…
MACHINES.hint: A thin edge that splits or cuts.
MACHINES.why: A blade is a wedge, a kind of inclined plane.

MACHINES.q: Which uses a lever to make lifting easier?
MACHINES.hint: A long bar you push on at one end.
MACHINES.why: A stick works as a lever.

MACHINES.q: A wheelchair ramp is a…
MACHINES.hint: It slopes up to the door.
MACHINES.why: A ramp is an inclined plane.

MACHINES.q: A doorknob turning a latch is a…
MACHINES.hint: A round handle turns a rod.
MACHINES.why: A doorknob is a wheel and axle.

MACHINES.q: An axe splitting firewood uses a…
MACHINES.hint: A thin edge pushes the wood apart.
MACHINES.why: An axe head is a wedge.

MACHINES.q: Raising a flag up a flagpole uses a…
MACHINES.hint: A rope goes over a wheel at the top.
MACHINES.why: A pulley lets you pull down to lift something up.

MACHINES.q: A playground slide is a kind of…
MACHINES.hint: It is a slope.
MACHINES.why: A slide is a sloped surface, an inclined plane.

MACHINES.q: A shovel lifting snow works as a…
MACHINES.hint: You push down on the handle to lift the blade.
MACHINES.why: A shovel is a lever.

MACHINES.q: A bike’s wheels and the rod through the middle are a…
MACHINES.hint: The wheel turns around a rod.
MACHINES.why: That is a wheel and axle.

MACHINES.q: Is it easier to push a heavy wagon up a long gentle ramp or a short steep one?
MACHINES.hint: A gentle slope needs less force, but you go farther.
MACHINES.why: A longer, gentler inclined plane needs less force.

MACHINES.q: The point a lever turns on is called the…
MACHINES.hint: On a seesaw it is the part in the middle.
MACHINES.why: A lever turns on a fulcrum.

MACHINES.q: Why does a long-handled shovel make digging easier?
MACHINES.a: a longer lever needs less force
MACHINES.hint: Longer levers help more.
MACHINES.why: A longer lever gives you more lifting power.

MACHINES.q: A pulley can let you lift something up by pulling…
MACHINES.hint: Think of a flag going up a pole.
MACHINES.why: A pulley changes the direction of your force.

MACHINES.q: A wedge works by…
MACHINES.hint: Think of an axe splitting wood.
MACHINES.why: A wedge’s thin edge pushes material apart.

MACHINES.q: A screw is really an inclined plane that is…
MACHINES.hint: Look at the ridges on a screw.
MACHINES.why: The thread of a screw is a ramp wrapped in a spiral.

MACHINES.q: Why is a road up a mountain zig-zagged instead of straight up?
MACHINES.a: a long, gentle slope is easier to climb
MACHINES.hint: It is like a long ramp.
MACHINES.why: A gentler inclined plane needs less force, even if it is longer.

MACHINES.q: Which simple machine has a rope over a wheel?
MACHINES.hint: Flagpoles have one at the top.
MACHINES.why: A pulley is a wheel with a rope or cable.

MACHINES.q: Which two simple machines are in a wheelbarrow?
MACHINES.a: a lever and a wheel and axle
MACHINES.hint: It has handles and a wheel.
MACHINES.why: The handles make a lever and the wheel turns on an axle.

MACHINES.q: Scissors are made of two…
MACHINES.hint: They turn on a pin, and the blades are sharp.
MACHINES.why: Scissors are two levers, and each blade is a wedge.

MACHINES.q: Which is a simple machine you use at the playground?
MACHINES.hint: It is a slope.
MACHINES.why: A slide is an inclined plane.

MACHINES.q: Which simple machine helps an elevator go up and down?
MACHINES.hint: Strong cables pass over wheels.
MACHINES.why: Elevators use pulleys and cables.

a push: pushing a friend on a swing
shoving a sled down a hill
hitting a baseball with a bat
pressing a button on a remote
squeezing toothpaste out of a tube
a pull: tugging a rope in tug of war
pulling a toboggan up a hill
picking an apple off a tree
pulling a carrot out of the garden

SENSES.q: A plant on a windowsill bends toward the window. It is responding to…
SENSES.hint: Plants need it to make food.
SENSES.why: Plants grow toward light.

SENSES.q: A deer lifts its head and runs when it hears a twig snap. It used its sense of…
SENSES.why: Animals use their senses to detect predators.

SENSES.q: Why do many birds fly south in the fall?
SENSES.a: to find food and warmer weather
SENSES.hint: Winter in Alberta is cold and food is hard to find.
SENSES.why: Migration is a response to temperature and food.

SENSES.q: A bear eats a lot in the fall and then sleeps most of the winter. This helps it…
SENSES.hint: There are few berries in winter.
SENSES.why: Animals respond to the seasons to survive.

SENSES.q: A wilted plant stands up again after it is watered. It responded to…
SENSES.why: Plants respond to water.

SENSES.q: Which helps protect wild animals?
SENSES.a: watching from a distance and not feeding them
SENSES.hint: How can we keep animals wild and safe?
SENSES.why: Watching quietly from a distance is respectful and safe.

SENSES.q: Why are there wildlife crossings over highways near Banff?
SENSES.hint: Animals need to move between habitats.
SENSES.why: Wildlife crossings protect animals and drivers.

SENSES.q: If all the grass disappeared, what would happen to the rabbits?
SENSES.hint: Plants and animals depend on each other.
SENSES.why: Animals depend on plants and other animals for food.

SENSES.q: A snowshoe hare turns white in winter. This helps it…
SENSES.why: White fur is camouflage in the snow.

SENSES.q: A dog sniffs the ground to find a treat. It is using its sense of…
SENSES.why: Dogs have an amazing sense of smell.

SENSES.q: You pull your hand away from a hot stove. You are responding to…
SENSES.why: Your sense of touch detects heat and keeps you safe.

SENSES.q: Sunflowers turn to face the sun. They respond to…
SENSES.why: Plants respond to light.

SENSES.q: A plant’s roots grow down toward…
SENSES.why: Roots grow toward water.

SENSES.q: Why do some animals, like gophers, hibernate?
SENSES.a: to save energy when there is little food
SENSES.hint: Winter is long and food is scarce.
SENSES.why: Hibernation saves energy through winter.

SENSES.q: Bees visit flowers because they…
SENSES.a: get nectar and pollen for food
SENSES.why: Bees feed on nectar and pollen and help plants make seeds.

SENSES.q: A turtle pulls into its shell when it is touched. This helps it…
SENSES.why: Hiding in its shell protects the turtle.

SENSES.q: An owl can hunt at night because it has great…
SENSES.hint: It must find a mouse in the dark.
SENSES.why: Owls use sharp eyes and ears to hunt at night.

SENSES.q: A cat’s whiskers help it…
SENSES.a: feel its way in tight spaces
SENSES.hint: Whiskers are very sensitive to touch.
SENSES.why: Whiskers help cats sense what is around them.

SENSES.q: In the fall, many leaves change colour and drop. The tree is responding to…
SENSES.why: Trees respond to the seasons by dropping their leaves.

SENSES.q: Geese fly in a V shape on their way south. They are…
SENSES.hint: They are going on a long trip.
SENSES.why: Migration is moving to a new place for the season.

SENSES.q: A bat finds bugs in the dark by…
SENSES.a: listening to echoes of its own sounds
SENSES.why: Bats use echolocation.

SENSES.q: A Venus flytrap snaps shut when a fly lands on it. It is responding to…
SENSES.why: Some plants respond to touch.

SENSES.q: A skunk sprays when it feels…
SENSES.hint: It is a way to protect itself.
SENSES.why: Skunks spray to scare away predators.

SENSES.q: Why do porcupines have quills?
SENSES.hint: Would you want to bite one?
SENSES.why: Sharp quills keep predators away.

SENSES.q: What does a seed need to start growing?
SENSES.hint: Think of planting seeds in spring.
SENSES.why: Seeds sprout when they get water, warmth and air.

SENSES.q: What do plants need to make their own food?
SENSES.why: Plants use sunlight, water and air to make food.

SENSES.q: An arctic fox has a white coat in winter and a brown coat in summer. This is called…
SENSES.hint: It helps the fox blend in.
SENSES.why: Changing colour helps the fox hide in each season.

SENSES.q: A gopher pops back into its hole when a hawk flies over. It saw the hawk’s…
SENSES.why: Animals use sight to spot danger.

SENSES.q: You smell smoke and leave the building. Which sense kept you safe?
SENSES.why: Our senses help us stay safe.

SENSES.q: Why should you never leave food out at a campsite in the Rockies?
SENSES.a: bears can smell it and come close
SENSES.why: Food smells attract bears, which is dangerous for people and bears.

SENSES.q: A plant left in a dark closet for a week turns pale and droopy. What does it need?
SENSES.why: Plants need light to stay healthy.

SENSES.q: A beaver slaps its tail on the water. It is…
SENSES.why: Beavers slap their tails to warn others.

EARTH.q: Which change to Earth’s surface happens very slowly?
EARTH.hint: It takes thousands of years.
EARTH.why: Wind, water and ice wear mountains down very slowly.

EARTH.q: Which change to Earth’s surface happens suddenly?
EARTH.hint: It can happen in minutes.
EARTH.why: Landslides, floods and earthquakes change the land quickly.

EARTH.q: Many of Alberta’s big rivers, like the Bow River, get water from…
EARTH.a: melting snow and glaciers in the Rockies
w: a big lake in the city
EARTH.hint: Rivers of ice high in the mountains.
EARTH.why: Snow and glacier meltwater from the mountains feed many Alberta rivers.

EARTH.q: The badlands near Drumheller were shaped mostly by…
EARTH.hint: Rain and wind wear away soft rock over a long time.
EARTH.why: Water and wind carved the badlands.

EARTH.q: A glacier is…
EARTH.a: a huge, slow-moving river of ice
EARTH.hint: You can see some in the Rocky Mountains.
EARTH.why: Glaciers are large masses of ice that move slowly.

EARTH.q: Which is a way people change Earth’s surface?
EARTH.hint: Think about what we build on land.
EARTH.why: Building, farming and mining all change the land.

EARTH.q: Mountain pine beetles change forests by…
EARTH.hint: They are tiny insects that live in trees.
EARTH.why: Mountain pine beetles can kill large areas of forest.

EARTH.q: Which is a way to take care of the land?
EARTH.hint: Stewardship means caring for the Earth.
EARTH.why: Picking up litter and planting trees help care for the land.

EARTH.q: Wearing away of rock and soil by water, wind or ice is called…
EARTH.hint: It starts with “e” and takes the land away bit by bit.
EARTH.why: Erosion carries rock and soil away.

EARTH.q: A big flood can change the land…
EARTH.hint: Calgary had a big flood in 2013.
EARTH.why: Floods are sudden changes to the land.

EARTH.q: Over a very long time, a river can carve…
w: a mountain on top of itself
EARTH.hint: Water keeps wearing away the rock.
EARTH.why: Rivers slowly cut valleys and canyons.

EARTH.q: Hoodoos in the badlands are…
EARTH.a: tall rock pillars shaped by erosion
EARTH.hint: They have a hard rock “cap” on top.
EARTH.why: Hoodoos form when soft rock wears away around a harder cap.

EARTH.q: Which is a sudden change to the land?
EARTH.hint: It happens in seconds.
EARTH.why: Earthquakes change the land suddenly.

EARTH.q: Planting trees on a hillside helps…
EARTH.a: roots hold the soil so it does not wash away
EARTH.hint: Roots are like nets.
EARTH.why: Plant roots help stop erosion.

EARTH.q: What carved the deep valleys in the Rocky Mountains long ago?
EARTH.hint: Giant rivers of ice.
EARTH.why: Moving glaciers scraped out wide valleys.

EARTH.q: An avalanche is…
EARTH.a: a sudden slide of snow down a mountain
EARTH.hint: It happens in seconds in the mountains.
EARTH.why: An avalanche is a sudden change.

EARTH.q: Why do farmers plant rows of trees beside their fields on the prairies?
EARTH.a: to stop the wind from blowing the soil away
w: to make shade for cows only
EARTH.hint: Wind can erode soil.
EARTH.why: Shelterbelts protect soil from wind erosion.

EARTH.q: Which helps protect a river bank from washing away?
EARTH.hint: Roots hold soil.
EARTH.why: Roots hold the soil in place.

EARTH.q: Mining and building roads are ways that…
EARTH.hint: Who drives the machines?
EARTH.why: Human activities change the land too.

EARTH.q: Beavers change the land by…
EARTH.hint: They chew trees and pile them in a stream.
EARTH.why: Beaver dams flood areas and create wetlands.

EARTH.q: A forest fire changes the land…
EARTH.hint: It can burn a forest in days.
EARTH.why: Fires are sudden changes, but forests slowly grow back.

EARTH.q: Which of these is a slow change to the land?
EARTH.a: a river bending into a new path over many years
EARTH.hint: It takes a long time.
EARTH.why: Rivers change course slowly.

EARTH.q: Recycling and composting help the Earth because…
EARTH.hint: Where does garbage go?
EARTH.why: Less garbage means less land used for landfills.

EARTH.q: Rocks tumbling in a river for a long time become…
EARTH.hint: Look at river pebbles.
EARTH.why: Water and rubbing wear rocks smooth.

EARTH.q: Why are there big rocks sitting alone on the prairie, like the Okotoks Big Rock?
EARTH.a: glaciers carried them there long ago
EARTH.hint: Ice can carry heavy things.
EARTH.why: Glaciers moved giant rocks and left them behind when they melted.

EARTH.q: Which weather can cause erosion?
EARTH.hint: Water and wind move soil.
EARTH.why: Rain and wind carry soil and rock away.

FOSSILS.q: A scientist who studies fossils is called a…
FOSSILS.a: paleontologist
FOSSILS.hint: It starts with “paleo”, which means old.
FOSSILS.why: Paleontologists study fossils.

FOSSILS.q: How do we know dinosaurs lived in Alberta long ago?
FOSSILS.a: their fossil bones were found here
FOSSILS.hint: What do paleontologists dig up?
FOSSILS.why: Fossilized bones show dinosaurs lived here millions of years ago.

FOSSILS.q: Rock layers lower down in the ground are usually…
FOSSILS.a: older
FOSSILS.hint: Layers pile up on top of each other over time.
FOSSILS.why: Lower layers formed first, so they are older.

FOSSILS.q: Long ago, the area that is now Alberta had…
FOSSILS.a: warm forests and an inland sea
FOSSILS.hint: Many dinosaur fossils come from swampy, warm places.
FOSSILS.why: Alberta was once warm, with forests and an inland sea.

FOSSILS.q: Which famous Alberta museum is full of dinosaur fossils?
FOSSILS.a: the Royal Tyrrell Museum
FOSSILS.hint: It is in Drumheller.
FOSSILS.why: The Royal Tyrrell Museum in Drumheller has one of the biggest dinosaur collections.

FOSSILS.q: Dinosaur Provincial Park is special because it is a…
FOSSILS.a: UNESCO World Heritage Site
FOSSILS.hint: It is protected for the whole world.
FOSSILS.why: It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with many fossils.

FOSSILS.q: Soil is made of…
FOSSILS.a: rock bits, living and dead things, air and water
FOSSILS.hint: Look closely at a handful from the garden.
FOSSILS.why: Soil has rock particles, organisms, air and water.

FOSSILS.q: How do earthworms change soil?
FOSSILS.a: they dig tunnels that let in air and water
FOSSILS.hint: Worms wiggle through the dirt.
FOSSILS.why: Worm tunnels mix soil and let air and water in.

FOSSILS.q: A dinosaur footprint in rock is a kind of…
FOSSILS.a: fossil
FOSSILS.hint: It is a trace of life from long ago.
FOSSILS.why: Footprints, bones, shells and leaf prints can all be fossils.

FOSSILS.q: Which is NOT a fossil?
FOSSILS.a: a plastic toy dinosaur
w: a dinosaur bone turned to stone
FOSSILS.hint: Fossils are real remains of living things.
FOSSILS.why: Fossils come from real plants and animals.

FOSSILS.q: Why do paleontologists dig very carefully with small brushes?
FOSSILS.a: so the fossils do not break
FOSSILS.hint: Fossils can be fragile.
FOSSILS.why: Careful digging protects fossils.

FOSSILS.q: Ammolite, a shiny gem from southern Alberta, comes from…
FOSSILS.a: fossil shells of sea animals
FOSSILS.hint: Alberta was once under a sea.
FOSSILS.why: Ammolite forms from fossil ammonite shells.

FOSSILS.q: Which soil holds water best for growing plants?
FOSSILS.a: soil with lots of dead leaves and plants mixed in
FOSSILS.hint: Rotting leaves act like a sponge.
FOSSILS.why: Soil rich in organic matter holds water well.

FOSSILS.q: If you find a fossil in a park, what should you do?
FOSSILS.a: leave it, take a photo and tell a ranger
FOSSILS.hint: In Alberta, fossils belong to everyone.
FOSSILS.why: Fossils are protected so scientists can study them.

FOSSILS.q: Which dinosaur was found in Alberta and named after the province?
FOSSILS.a: Albertosaurus
FOSSILS.hint: The name has Alberta in it.
FOSSILS.why: Albertosaurus was a meat-eater that lived in Alberta.

FOSSILS.q: What do fossils tell us?
FOSSILS.a: what living things were like long ago
w: what the weather will be tomorrow
FOSSILS.hint: They are clues from the past.
FOSSILS.why: Fossils show us plants and animals from long ago.

FOSSILS.q: Most fossils are found in which kind of rock?
FOSSILS.a: rock made from layers of mud and sand
FOSSILS.hint: Layers pile up and squeeze together.
FOSSILS.why: Fossils form in sedimentary rock made from layers.

FOSSILS.q: A paleontologist finds a big, sharp tooth. The dinosaur probably ate…
FOSSILS.a: meat
FOSSILS.hint: Sharp teeth tear meat.
FOSSILS.why: Sharp, pointed teeth belong to meat-eaters.

FOSSILS.q: A paleontologist finds flat, grinding teeth. The dinosaur probably ate…
FOSSILS.a: plants
FOSSILS.hint: Cows have flat teeth for chewing grass.
FOSSILS.why: Flat teeth are good for grinding plants.

FOSSILS.q: Which of these could become a fossil?
FOSSILS.a: a fish skeleton buried in mud
FOSSILS.hint: Fossils come from real living things.
FOSSILS.why: Bones buried in mud can become fossils.

FOSSILS.q: Dinosaurs lived…
FOSSILS.a: millions of years ago, before people
w: at the same time as cavemen
FOSSILS.hint: No person ever saw a living dinosaur.
FOSSILS.why: Dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.

FOSSILS.q: A fossil of a seashell found on a mountain tells us…
FOSSILS.a: the land was once under the sea
FOSSILS.hint: Where do shells usually live?
FOSSILS.why: Sea fossils on land show that the area was once covered by water.

FOSSILS.q: Why is topsoil important?
FOSSILS.a: plants grow in it
w: it is good for building rockets
FOSSILS.hint: Farms need good soil.
FOSSILS.why: Topsoil has the nutrients plants need.

FOSSILS.q: Compost helps soil by…
FOSSILS.a: adding rotted food and leaves that feed plants
FOSSILS.hint: Old banana peels turn into…
FOSSILS.why: Compost adds nutrients to soil.

FOSSILS.q: Which soil feels gritty and lets water drain fast?
FOSSILS.a: sandy soil
FOSSILS.hint: It is like the beach.
FOSSILS.why: Sandy soil has big grains, so water drains quickly.

FOSSILS.q: Which soil is sticky and holds water for a long time?
FOSSILS.a: clay soil
FOSSILS.hint: You can mould it into shapes.
FOSSILS.why: Clay has tiny particles that hold water.

FOSSILS.q: A trace fossil is…
FOSSILS.a: a sign left by a living thing, like a footprint
FOSSILS.hint: It is not a bone.
FOSSILS.why: Footprints, nests and burrows are trace fossils.

FOSSILS.q: Which tool would a paleontologist use first to clean dirt off a fossil?
FOSSILS.a: a soft brush
FOSSILS.hint: Be gentle.
FOSSILS.why: Brushes remove dirt without damaging the fossil.

FOSSILS.q: Where would you find the oldest fossils in a cliff of rock layers?
FOSSILS.a: near the bottom
FOSSILS.hint: Bottom layers formed first.
FOSSILS.why: Lower layers are older, so they hold older fossils.

FOSSILS.q: Hadrosaurs, often found in Alberta, were called duck-billed dinosaurs because…
FOSSILS.a: their mouths were shaped like a duck’s bill
w: they had feathers like a duck
FOSSILS.hint: Look at the shape of the snout.
FOSSILS.why: Hadrosaurs had wide, flat, bill-shaped snouts.

mud and sand cover the bones
layers pile up and turn to rock
wind and water wear the rock away
a paleontologist digs it up

a sea animal dies
its shell sinks to the sea floor
sand and mud bury the shell
the layers slowly turn to rock
the shell’s shape is left in stone

spot a bone in the rock
brush the dirt away carefully
wrap it in plaster to protect it
carry it to the museum lab
clean and study it

How does soil form? Put the steps in order.
a big rock sits in the open
rain, ice and wind crack the rock
the rock breaks into tiny bits
dead plants and leaves mix in
worms mix it into rich soil
Start with rock. How does it get broken up?
How does a river make a valley? Put the steps in order.
rain and melting snow fill a stream
the water flows downhill
the water carries away bits of rock
over many years the stream cuts deeper
a valley forms
Start with the water. What does flowing water do to the rock?
Rock layers in the badlands: put them from oldest to newest.
the bottom layer
the middle layer
the top layer
Layers pile up one on top of another.
How does an ammolite gem form? Put the steps in order.
an ammonite lives in an ancient sea
it dies and sinks to the sea floor
mud buries its shell
over millions of years it turns to stone
people dig up the shiny gem
Start with the living sea animal.
How do hoodoos form? Put the steps in order.
layers of soft rock build up
a hard rock layer sits on top
rain and wind wear away the soft rock
the hard cap protects the rock below it
a tall pillar is left standing
Start with the layers. What wears away?
How does a footprint become a fossil? Put the steps in order.
a dinosaur steps in soft mud
the mud dries in the sun
sand blows in and fills the print
layers turn to rock
erosion uncovers the footprint
Start with the step. How is the print saved?
A fossil goes to the museum. Put the steps in order.
a hiker spots a bone
they tell the museum
paleontologists dig it out
the bone is cleaned in the lab
it goes on display
Start with the discovery.
How does compost become soil? Put the steps in order.
you put food scraps in the bin
worms and tiny living things eat them
the scraps rot and break down
it turns into dark compost
you mix it into the garden
Start with the scraps.

snow piles up in the mountains
it packs down into thick ice
the glacier slowly slides downhill
it scrapes the rock beneath it
a wide U-shaped valley is left

pour the juice into a jug
put it in the blue bin
put the gift in a box
Take a photo with a tablet
point it at what you want
fill a bucket with wet sand
put the lid on and blend
fold the corners to the middle
put the bag in the microwave
wait for the popping to stop

CS.q: Breaking a big job into small steps is called…
CS.hint: You take a big problem apart into pieces.
CS.why: Breaking a problem into parts is called decomposition.

CS.q: A robot is told: forward 2, turn left, forward 1. Instead it turns right. What should you do?
CS.a: find the step that is wrong and fix it
CS.hint: Debugging means finding the mistake.
CS.why: Working back to find and fix a mistake is called debugging.

CS.q: Can there be more than one right way to solve a problem?
CS.hint: Think of different routes to school.
CS.why: Creative thinking finds different ways to reach the same goal.

CS.q: The Canadarm is a famous Canadian invention used…
CS.a: on the space shuttle and space station
CS.hint: It is a robot arm.
CS.why: The Canadarm is a robot arm that worked in space.

CS.q: Spotting that “red, blue, red, blue” repeats is called…
CS.hint: Something that happens again and again.
CS.why: Noticing repeats is pattern recognition.

CS.q: An algorithm is…
CS.hint: A recipe is one.
CS.why: An algorithm is a list of steps to follow.

CS.q: A recipe says “bake, then mix, then pour”. What is wrong?
CS.a: the steps are in the wrong order
CS.hint: Can you bake something before you mix it?
CS.why: Order matters in an algorithm. You must mix and pour before baking.

CS.q: Instead of writing “clap, clap, clap, clap”, a coder could write…
CS.hint: A loop repeats steps.
CS.why: A loop repeats steps so you do not write them again and again.

CS.q: “If it is raining, take an umbrella.” This kind of instruction is a…
CS.hint: It only happens IF something is true.
CS.why: A condition decides what to do based on what is true.

CS.q: A robot must get from the door to the desk. Why test the steps before running them for real?
CS.hint: Fixing a mistake early is easier.
CS.why: Testing helps find bugs before they cause problems.

CS.q: What comes next in the pattern: square, circle, square, circle, …?
CS.hint: Look at what repeats.
CS.why: The pattern repeats square, circle.

CS.q: Which is an example of decomposing a problem?
CS.a: cleaning your room one corner at a time
CS.hint: Break a big job into small parts.
CS.why: Breaking a big job into smaller parts is decomposition.

CS.q: Your friend’s steps to draw a house forgot the roof. Fixing it is called…
CS.hint: Finding and fixing a mistake.
CS.why: Debugging is finding and fixing errors.

CS.q: Who can be a coder?
w: only people with a computer at home
CS.hint: You are learning right now!
CS.why: Anyone can learn to code with practice.

CS.q: A loop in a program…
CS.hint: Loop means go around again.
CS.why: Loops repeat instructions.

CS.q: A bug in a program is…
CS.hint: It makes the program do the wrong thing.
CS.why: A bug is an error in the instructions.

CS.q: “If the light is red, stop. Otherwise, go.” What does the robot do at a green light?
CS.hint: Green is not red.
CS.why: The condition is false, so the robot does the “otherwise” part.

CS.q: A robot starts facing north. It turns right once. Which way is it facing?
CS.hint: North is up. Turn clockwise.
CS.why: Turning right from north points east.

CS.q: A robot starts facing north. It turns right twice. Which way is it facing?
CS.hint: Two right turns make a U-turn.
CS.why: Two right turns point the robot the opposite way.

CS.q: Which is the best first step to solve a big problem?
CS.hint: Small steps are easier.
CS.why: Decomposing makes big problems manageable.

CS.q: A program uses “repeat 3 times: jump”. How many jumps happen?
CS.hint: Count the repeats.
CS.why: The loop runs the jump 3 times.

CS.q: A program uses “repeat 2 times: clap, stomp”. What happens?
CS.hint: Do the whole inside part, then do it again.
CS.why: The loop repeats both steps in order, twice.

CS.q: An input is information that goes INTO a computer. Which is an input?
CS.hint: You give it to the computer.
CS.why: Keyboards, mice and microphones are inputs.

CS.q: An output is information that comes OUT of a computer. Which is an output?
CS.hint: The computer gives it to you.
CS.why: Screens, speakers and printers are outputs.

CS.q: Why should code be tested many times with different inputs?
CS.a: to make sure it works in every case
CS.hint: Maybe it works for one case but not another.
CS.why: Testing with different inputs catches hidden bugs.

CS.q: Which instruction is clearest for a robot?
CS.hint: Robots need exact instructions.
CS.why: Computers follow exact, precise instructions.

CS.q: Sorting your hockey cards by team is a way of…
CS.hint: You are putting information into groups.
CS.why: Grouping and sorting helps us organize data.

CS.q: Why should you keep your passwords secret?
CS.hint: Who should be able to log in as you?
CS.why: Secret passwords protect your information.

CS.q: A traffic light changes red, green, yellow, red, green, yellow. What kind of thinking spots this?
CS.hint: Something repeats.
CS.why: Spotting repeats is pattern recognition.

CS.q: Which of these is a computer?
CS.hint: Lots of things have tiny computers inside.
CS.why: Laptops, phones, tablets and many toys all have computers inside.

SCI_METHOD.q: What is a prediction?
SCI_METHOD.a: a smart guess about what will happen
SCI_METHOD.hint: You make it before you test.
SCI_METHOD.why: A prediction is what you think will happen, based on what you know.

SCI_METHOD.q: You test which ball bounces highest. To make it a fair test, you should…
SCI_METHOD.a: drop every ball from the same height
w: drop each ball from a different height
throw the balls as hard as you can
SCI_METHOD.hint: Change only one thing: the ball.
SCI_METHOD.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.

SCI_METHOD.q: You want to know which mitten keeps a hand warmest. What should you change?
SCI_METHOD.a: only the kind of mitten
SCI_METHOD.hint: Change just one thing.
SCI_METHOD.why: Change one thing (the mitten) and keep the rest the same.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which tool measures how long a pencil is?
SCI_METHOD.a: a ruler
SCI_METHOD.hint: It has centimetre marks.
SCI_METHOD.why: A ruler measures length.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which tool measures how hot or cold the water is?
SCI_METHOD.a: a thermometer
SCI_METHOD.hint: It shows degrees Celsius.
SCI_METHOD.why: A thermometer measures temperature.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which tool compares which rock is heavier?
SCI_METHOD.a: a balance
SCI_METHOD.hint: It has two pans that tip.
SCI_METHOD.why: A balance compares mass.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which tool helps you see tiny details on a bug?
SCI_METHOD.a: a magnifying glass
SCI_METHOD.hint: It makes things look bigger.
SCI_METHOD.why: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger.

SCI_METHOD.q: Why do scientists write down what they observe?
SCI_METHOD.a: so they remember and can share it
SCI_METHOD.hint: Memories can be wrong.
SCI_METHOD.why: Recording results helps scientists remember, compare and share.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which is a question you can test?
SCI_METHOD.a: Which paper towel soaks up the most water?
w: Why is blue the best colour?
SCI_METHOD.hint: You could do an experiment to find out.
SCI_METHOD.why: A testable question can be answered by doing a test and measuring.

SCI_METHOD.q: Your results do not match your prediction. What should you do?
SCI_METHOD.a: say what really happened and think about why
SCI_METHOD.hint: Scientists are honest.
SCI_METHOD.why: Unexpected results are useful. Report them honestly.

SCI_METHOD.q: You test a toy car on 3 ramps. Why run each test 3 times?
SCI_METHOD.a: to make sure the results are the same each time
SCI_METHOD.hint: One try could be a fluke.
SCI_METHOD.why: Repeating a test makes the results more trustworthy.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which is an observation?
SCI_METHOD.a: The ice cube melted in 10 minutes.
w: I think the ice will melt fast.
SCI_METHOD.hint: Something you saw or measured.
SCI_METHOD.why: An observation is what you notice with your senses or measure.

SCI_METHOD.q: A table and a bar graph are good ways to…
SCI_METHOD.a: show your results
SCI_METHOD.hint: They organize numbers.
SCI_METHOD.why: Tables and graphs make results easy to read and compare.

SCI_METHOD.q: What is a conclusion?
SCI_METHOD.a: what you learned from your results
SCI_METHOD.hint: It comes at the end.
SCI_METHOD.why: A conclusion answers your question using your evidence.

SCI_METHOD.q: Before mixing things in an experiment, you should…
SCI_METHOD.a: ask an adult and wear safety glasses if needed
SCI_METHOD.hint: Safety first.
SCI_METHOD.why: Scientists stay safe by following rules and asking for help.

SCI_METHOD.q: You test which surface makes a sled go farthest. What do you measure?
SCI_METHOD.a: how far the sled goes
SCI_METHOD.hint: What does your question ask about?
SCI_METHOD.why: Measure the thing your question is about.

SCI_METHOD.q: You grow two bean plants. One gets light and one is kept in the dark. What are you testing?
SCI_METHOD.a: whether plants need light
SCI_METHOD.hint: What is different between the two plants?
SCI_METHOD.why: The only difference is light, so that is what you are testing.

SCI_METHOD.q: In the bean plant test, what should stay the same for both plants?
SCI_METHOD.a: the water, soil and pot size
w: only the colour of the pot
SCI_METHOD.hint: Everything except the thing you are testing.
SCI_METHOD.why: Keep everything else the same so the test is fair.

SCI_METHOD.q: Evidence is…
SCI_METHOD.a: facts and measurements that support an idea
SCI_METHOD.hint: It is what you saw and measured.
SCI_METHOD.why: Evidence comes from observations and measurements.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which unit would you use to record a temperature?
SCI_METHOD.a: degrees Celsius (°C)
SCI_METHOD.hint: Thermometers in Canada use it.
SCI_METHOD.why: Temperature in Canada is measured in degrees Celsius.

SCI_METHOD.q: You want to know if salt helps ice melt faster. Which is the fair test?
SCI_METHOD.a: two ice cubes the same size, salt on one only
w: a big ice cube with salt and a tiny one without
one ice cube in the freezer and one outside
SCI_METHOD.hint: Only one thing should be different.
SCI_METHOD.why: Same size, same place, only the salt is different.

SCI_METHOD.q: Why should scientists share their results?
SCI_METHOD.a: so others can learn and check them
SCI_METHOD.hint: Science is teamwork.
SCI_METHOD.why: Sharing lets others learn from and repeat the test.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which of these is a good way to share your results?
SCI_METHOD.a: a poster with a graph
SCI_METHOD.hint: Other people need to see them.
SCI_METHOD.why: Posters, talks and reports share what you found.

SCI_METHOD.q: You drop a feather and a rock. You see the rock land first. This is…
SCI_METHOD.a: an observation
SCI_METHOD.hint: You saw it happen.
SCI_METHOD.why: Something you see happen is an observation.

SCI_METHOD.q: “I think the bigger magnet will pick up more paper clips.” This is…
SCI_METHOD.a: a prediction
SCI_METHOD.hint: It says what you think will happen.
SCI_METHOD.why: A prediction is made before testing.

SCI_METHOD.q: You counted 12 paper clips on the big magnet and 5 on the small one. Your conclusion is…
SCI_METHOD.a: the big magnet picked up more paper clips
w: the small magnet is broken for sure
SCI_METHOD.hint: What do your numbers show?
SCI_METHOD.why: A conclusion uses the results: 12 is more than 5.

SCI_METHOD.q: What should you do first in an investigation?
SCI_METHOD.a: ask a question
SCI_METHOD.hint: What do you want to find out?
SCI_METHOD.why: Every investigation starts with a question.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which sense would you use to observe if a fabric is soft?
SCI_METHOD.a: touch
SCI_METHOD.hint: Use your fingers.
SCI_METHOD.why: Touch tells you how something feels.

SCI_METHOD.q: Why is it NOT safe to taste things in a science test?
SCI_METHOD.a: some materials can make you sick
w: food is never used in science
SCI_METHOD.hint: You do not always know what is in it.
SCI_METHOD.why: Never taste materials unless an adult says it is safe.

SCI_METHOD.q: You measure a plant every Monday for 4 weeks. The best way to show how it grew is…
SCI_METHOD.a: a table or a graph
SCI_METHOD.hint: You have 4 numbers to compare.
SCI_METHOD.why: Tables and graphs show changes over time.

SCI_METHOD.q: A scientist changes the amount of water each plant gets. The amount of water is the thing being…
SCI_METHOD.a: tested
SCI_METHOD.hint: It is the one thing that is different.
SCI_METHOD.why: The thing you change on purpose is what you are testing.

SCI_METHOD.q: Which question could you answer with a fair test at home?
SCI_METHOD.a: Does ice melt faster in water or in air?
SCI_METHOD.hint: You could measure it with a timer.
SCI_METHOD.why: You can measure melting time to answer it.
